findings.title: Shallow malformed XML can bypass admission and overflow the DOM parser stack
findings.summary:
Malformed unquoted attributes can make tolerant package admission observe shallow XML while the permissive DOM constructs deeply nested elements without a depth guard. Repeated sibling

tags are one framing; a=x followed by b="x>..." can expose attribute-contained tags as another. Rendering is the earlier affected route; WmlDocument::from_bytes followed by lazy main_document is the newly supplied route. Strict checked inspection rejects the malformed attribute form. A further supplied shallow sibling framing, x>, makes the DOM swallow the closing tag as attribute text and treat following siblings as descendants.
findings.remediation: Make tolerant attribute tokenization identical between admission and DOM construction or refuse unsupported unquoted values, and enforce a real construction-depth limit or use an iterative DOM parser.

findings.title: Reading or converting nested legacy DOC fields can monopolize the processing thread
findings.summary: An attacker-authored Word 97–2003 DOC can repeatedly begin fields and enter their result sections, leaving an increasingly long all-false field stack. Story::blocks scans the entire stack before every input character, giving quadratic CPU work during reading/conversion and even the native Word-input refusal hint. Assigned discovery-0031 supplies a balanced result-state framing with approximately 100000 nested fields in a few hundred kilobytes, implying billions of boolean inspections. This is heap-stack scanning CPU cost, not recursive call-stack overflow.
findings.remediation: Maintain an O(1) active-code-frame count, updating it correctly on begin, separator and end while preserving suppression under any code ancestor. Enforce explicit field-nesting and processing-work budgets for balanced and malformed legacy field streams before excessive work. Keep legacy diagnostic probes cheap and bounded, or enforce the same field/work budgets before invoking the full reader solely for a refusal hint.

findings.title: Large Chicago numbering values can exhaust memory while reading or rendering a DOCX
findings.summary:
An untrusted DOCX can select Chicago numbering with a huge list start/startOverride or section page start. The shared chicago_label formatter repeats a UTF-8 symbol roughly n/4 times without a length bound, allowing gigabyte allocations during list rendering, ordinary section-page processing and Markdown numbered-list views. Authored endnote starts also reach this shared formatter. The supplied u32::MAX framing selects 1073741824 double-daggers, about 3 GiB of UTF-8 label bytes; this is static arithmetic. Additional supplied static framing: start=2147483647 selects 536870912 UTF-8 double-daggers (‡), requesting 1.5 GiB of marker bytes before downstream copies.
 Assigned discovery-0032 additionally supplies start=4294967294: 1073741824 daggers (†), about 3 GiB of UTF-8 before copies. Level-zero reader/agent labels reach the shared formatter without a large ilvl.
findings.remediation:
Bound generated byte/glyph length inside the shared Chicago formatter before repetition, with a documented safe cycle/fallback or typed refusal. Apply that bound to all list, startOverride, section-page and Markdown/direct list_number callers; do not rely on input bytes, counter saturation or later clipping. Include authored endnote numStart/format and MCP agent-view callers in the shared formatter budget.
Additional retained remediation detail: Apply a central maximum output length to Chicago labels before repetition and enforce a cumulative numbering-output budget. Use a documented bounded fallback or typed refusal consistently for list, read/agent, page and future formatter consumers.

findings.title: Aliased legacy DOC pieces expand small physical text into enormous logical stories
findings.summary:
Thousands of contiguous logical pieces can all reference the same physical text range. For example, 4095 pieces referencing one common 1 MiB compressed-text range describe nearly 4 GiB of logical characters while requiring only roughly 49 KiB of piece records. main_text materializes metadata for every character, requiring tens of GiB before rendering. A second source-derived framing uses approximately 65,535 pieces reusing 64 KiB, producing over four billion logical characters from a piece table below 1 MiB; expansion precedes later auxiliary-table checks. The assigned 1024-by-65536 framing yields 67108864 logical characters and at least 768 MiB for char/CP/FC fields alone, before modifiers and allocation/output overhead; these are static counts, not measurements. Supplied discovery-0023 additionally gives 4096 contiguous one-million-character pieces sharing a 1 MB physical range (4096000000 logical characters within u32). Public read/conversion and native read_document refusal-hint parsing reach the same expansion before returning a format diagnostic; no runtime resource measurement is claimed. Additional supplied static framing: 4096 pieces reusing one 64 KiB compressed extent describe 268435456 logical characters; continuity and source-bound checks permit the reuse. This is not a measured allocation. Assigned discovery-0031 supplies 4000 one-million-character logical pieces sharing about 1 MB of physical text with about 48 KB of piece metadata, requesting about four billion StoryChars. CP continuity, checked offsets and physically bounded CFB traversal do not bound logical expansion; counts are static.
 Assigned discovery-0032 supplies 65535 contiguous pieces of 65535 compressed characters sharing one 65535-byte physical range: 4294836225 logical CPs within u32 and about 786 KB of piece records. These are static counts.
findings.remediation:
Introduce configurable legacy physical-input, piece-count, cumulative logical-character, retained-metadata and expansion-work budgets. Check FIB ccp_text and checked cumulative piece lengths before materialization, charge every decoded character including repeated physical aliases, and return typed refusals through read/doc_to_markdown/doc_to_docx and CLI callers. Preserve legitimate fast-save aliases and split UTF-16 surrogate handling within budget. Replace full legacy parsing used only for diagnostic refusal hints with a cheap bounded probe, or apply the same logical/work budgets before that parser runs.
Additional retained remediation detail: Introduce a configurable legacy logical-character/output budget, check ccp_text and cumulative decoded piece work before materialization, and enforce it during decoding. Preserve valid reuse while returning a typed refusal for excessive expansion.

findings.title: ZIP footer and count interpretation mismatch bypasses entry-count admission
findings.summary: The independent preindex footer parser can count a different EOCD or count field from zip 9.0.5. False small-count EOCDs in valid comments can be skipped by zip; a same-footer total=3/on-this-disk=10001 also passes max_entries=10000 while zip indexes 10001. ZIP64 size/offset triggers differ too. Neither admission nor PartFs enforces the actual opened count; duplicate detection also trusts the unrelated declared count. Another supplied false-footer proof uses an EOCD-shaped record inside the real archive comment whose own comment length is impossible; preindex trusts its low count while the ZIP reader rejects it and backtracks.
findings.remediation: Use the delegated reader's authoritative validated EOCD/ZIP64 selection, consistent ZIP32 total/per-disk fields and all ZIP64 total/size/offset triggers. Bound raw central-record traversal/count before index allocation, reject inconsistent unsupported metadata, and retain a post-open active archive.len cap as defense in depth; that later check cannot undo earlier allocation. Reconcile selected raw counts with indexed counts for exact duplicates, including name collapse, comments, ZIP64 and prepended data. Detect raw exact-name duplicates directly or through the reader's duplicate flag rather than relying solely on a count-shortfall inference.

findings.title: npm plan recording follows a predictable staging symlink
findings.summary: When recording plan operations, the npm CLI writes to a basename/PID staging path without exclusive creation. A local attacker who can create entries in that directory can redirect the write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI user.
findings.remediation: Create an unpredictable private staging directory next to the plan and open the staged regular file exclusively. Write through its held descriptor and rename only that file. At minimum refuse every preexisting staging entry using exclusive creation rather than default truncating writes.

findings.title: Repeated HTML chunk references bypass conversion memory budgets
findings.summary: A DOCX can repeatedly reference one modest HTML part. The renderer admits the small original package, then copies and converts that chunk separately for every reference and concatenates all generated XML. The resulting allocation and work can exceed package budgets by orders of magnitude. For example, 10,000 short references to one 1 MiB ordinary HTML paragraph can imply roughly 10 GiB of generated XML; this is a static estimate, not a runtime measurement. The assigned source also supplies nested HTML tables as a depth variant of this post-admission expansion boundary: generated WML enters unchecked DOM and recursive table layout. Complete repair must enforce both cumulative size/work and generated depth; the earlier dedicated depth record remains cross-referenced.
findings.remediation: Make altChunk expansion fallible under active cumulative expanded-byte, node/element, depth, work and occurrence budgets. Check contributions before conversion/allocation/append, including repeated internal relationships and MIME-decoded chunks, and validate generated XML under active limits before DOM construction. Caching may reduce repeated conversion CPU but cannot replace the total-output budget.

findings.title: Public Strict-format probe inflates unbounded document headers
findings.summary: The public main_part_is_strict helper reads word/document.xml without admission or an inflation/preamble cap. A compressible oversized/unfinished root opening tag or long XML comment keeps the last '<' at offset zero; the full growing head remains retained and is repeatedly scanned until the root tag completes or EOF, allowing memory/CPU exhaustion for direct library consumers. The assigned audit establishes direct public-library exposure and found no in-repository production caller; ordinary rendering is not claimed to call this detector.
findings.remediation: Apply bounded admission before indexing/inflation and explicit cumulative inflated-byte/preamble/work limits to this public helper. Use a streaming lexical probe with bounded retained state for comments, declarations and chunk-spanning root tags; refuse excessive probes with a checked/limited API and safe default limits.

findings.title: Unbounded document table spans exhaust memory during rendering
findings.summary: Untrusted direct OOXML gridSpan/gridBefore/gridAfter and imported HTML/MHT colspan values become unrestricted output column counts. Tiny metadata can request a billion columns, driving dense column/preference/merge vectors or pre-DOM gridCol XML generation before derived-output budgets. These independently reachable paths require controls before both import generation and layout; package byte/depth admission does not bound their semantic expansion.
findings.remediation: Enforce practical per-cell span/row-skip and checked cumulative table/grid/output budgets across direct OOXML gridSpan/gridBefore/gridAfter and HTML/MHT colspan. Apply the common limit before HTML generation and before RawCell, column/preference/merge allocation or span-sized work; use checked sums and col+span arithmetic and return a typed conversion refusal. Neither importer-only nor later layout-only checking is sufficient. Use fallible allocation/reservation within those bounds so capacity failures become typed refusals. Carry the caller-configurable column/occupancy budget through every table source and enforce a generated-XML/output ceiling before altChunk materialization.

findings.title: Repeated relationship IDs trigger quadratic repair work
findings.summary: Opening a package repairs identical duplicate relationship IDs. For n distinct IDs each repeated identically, each repair linearly searches an increasingly long Vec, producing quadratic CPU work on shallow metadata that fits existing byte and attribute limits. Assigned discovery-0031 supplies approximately 200000 shallow Relationship records with 100000 distinct identical duplicate pairs within a 64 MiB part, implying about five billion membership comparisons. Conflicting duplicates remain promptly refused; counts are static.
findings.remediation: Track already-reported duplicate IDs in a HashSet or alongside seen-map state, retaining a Vec only for deterministic reporting order. Optionally cap relationship-record/work totals before repair; test many distinct identical duplicate pairs while preserving deterministic repaired-ID order and conflicting-duplicate refusals. Apply an active relationship-record/work budget at metadata admission in addition to making duplicate membership near-linear.

findings.title: Unbounded list levels cause billions of iterations or allocations
findings.summary:
Paragraph and numbering-definition ilvl attributes accept arbitrary u32 values. Resolving an undefined high level scans every lower integer; defining the high level instead drives counter initialization and label substitution loops over the same enormous range. Abstract definitions and full lvlOverride records accept the same unchecked level IDs; both missing-level reverse search and defined-level counter/label work require bounded handling.
 Assigned discovery-0032 preserves the valid numbering-instance prerequisite and the distinct billion-level defined-counter variant as well as undefined-level backwards search.
findings.remediation:
Validate the supported ilvl domain in paragraph, style, abstract and override sources before use. Find fallback levels among actual defined keys and initialize/substitute only supported or defined levels; avoid any iteration or allocation proportional to an untrusted numeric level. Return a typed refusal for unsupported level metadata rather than attempting dense counter or placeholder materialization.
Additional retained remediation detail: Validate paragraph and numbering-definition level IDs against the supported 0..=8 range. Resolve ancestors by actual defined keys and bound synthesized counters and marker iteration independently of untrusted integer values.

findings.title: Converting legacy DOC text with a long numeric prefix causes quadratic work
findings.summary: For each period or closing parenthesis, the Markdown escaper rescans the full preceding text. A long digit prefix followed by many periods repeatedly scans the same digits, consuming disproportionate CPU on a small legacy DOC.
findings.remediation: Track a running all-ASCII-digits prefix flag while iterating once, or identify the sole initial numeric-list delimiter once. Preserve escaping behavior with linear work.

findings.title: Ragged legacy DOC tables expand into an unbounded padded rectangle
findings.summary: A table with one wide row and many narrow rows contains relatively few cells, but legacy Markdown serialization emits the widest row's cell count for every row. Compact input can therefore generate gigabytes of output and exhaust importer memory. The same unbounded serialization is independently exposed through public to_markdown(LegacyDocument), in addition to DOC byte conversions. Assigned discovery-0031 supplies a static 100000-cell row plus 100000 short/empty rows framing: about ten billion serialized cells before DOCX admission. No numeric colspan forgery or logical-piece alias is required.
findings.remediation: Before rectangularizing a table, use checked multiplication to enforce a generated-cell quota and enforce cumulative output-byte/work limits. Refuse over-budget tables with a typed error. Enforce a supported column ceiling and cover doc_to_markdown and doc_to_docx's Markdown intermediate; a bounded sparse representation is another option.

findings.title: Privacy scrubbing can return identifying data in valid relocated DOCX parts
findings.summary: A document returned successfully by scrub can retain creator/editor identities, company/custom properties, revision authors, session IDs and people information when valid OPC relationships locate those parts outside conventional filenames or word/. Sharing the supposedly scrubbed output discloses the retained data. Supported relocated stories include content/main.xml and word/main.dat; a conventional prefix or .xml suffix is not semantic part identity.
findings.remediation: Discover all applicable metadata, people, comments, settings and story parts through relationships and content types. Apply the requested transforms to every discovered part and assert privacy-specific postconditions before returning success.
